title: A homepage for a product with three audiences
metaTitle: Write the homepage for who pays
excerpt: Pick the audience that pays and write the first screen for them. The other audiences get a labeled path. A homepage that greets everyone in the hero greets no one.
alt: A person in a blue shirt signing a paper document with a pen, one decision on the page the way a homepage should decide who it is for.
caption: One signature. Write the first screen for the audience that pays. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How do you choose which audience the homepage speaks to?
faqs.answer: Rank the audiences by who can say yes to the money. Write the first screen for that person, with their noun, their proof, and one action. Give the others a text link to a page that speaks to them in the first paragraph.

faqs.question: What is wrong with three equal buttons in the hero?
faqs.answer: Equal buttons are the compromise of greeting everyone, moved into the component. People decide in the first seconds whether the page is for them. One primary action for the paying audience, and specific text links for the others, is a decision they can read.

faqs.question: Where should investors, press, or job candidates go?
faqs.answer: Give them the footer or a single about link. The homepage is a selling page. A press kit can exist without occupying the first screen, and an origin story belongs there only when it changes the decision to buy.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A homepage with three audiences still has one first screen. Pick the audience that pays, and write that screen for them. The other two can have a path, a link, and a sentence. A multi audience homepage that tries to greet everyone in the hero greets no one, because nobody can tell the page is for them.

Decide who pays before you debate the headline. Revenue, frequency, and whether you can serve them well all count. The audience you like narrating is not automatically the audience the first screen should serve.

## Name the three, then rank them

Write the three audiences in the customer's language. A clinic software company might have the practice owner, the office manager, and the clinician. A goods brand might have the person who buys, the person who receives a gift, and the wholesale buyer. A studio's client might have a champion inside the company, a finance partner, and the end user of the thing being built.

Rank them by who can say yes to the money. The practice owner may pay even if the clinician lives in the product all day. The wholesale buyer may keep the factory busy even if the retail page is the one you enjoy. Put the paying audience first. Give the daily user a path that proves you understand the product. Give the third audience a path that keeps them from feeling excluded, without letting them rewrite the hero.

If two audiences pay equally, pick the one whose decision is slower to undo, or the one you can serve completely today. A homepage that alternates heroes by campaign is still one homepage at a time. Rotation is not a substitute for a rank.

Write one sentence each: what they came to do. "See if this replaces our booking book." "Check the wholesale terms." "Watch a clinician finish a note." Those sentences become the hero, the secondary link, and the third link. If you cannot write the sentence, you do not yet know the audience. Do not invent a headline to cover the gap.

## The first screen is a decision

The first screen carries the paying audience's sentence, the proof they need, and one action. Nielsen Norman Group's research on how long people stay is the constraint. Users often leave in 10 to 20 seconds. A clear value has to be visible in about 10 seconds if you want a longer visit. Three slogans stacked in the hero spend that window on diplomacy.

Use their noun. If they say "clinics," say clinics. If they say "independent bookshops," say that. A category word chosen to include all three audiences usually includes none of them. You can mention the others in a single line under the action: "Wholesale terms" and "For clinicians" as text links, not as equal buttons.

Google's guidance on title links asks for one obvious main heading, and for a title element that describes the page. A homepage whose title tries to list every audience becomes boilerplate. Put the paying audience and the offer in the title. Let the other paths be visible on the page without crowding the title.

Proof on that first screen should be proof for the payer. A number you can stand behind, a named customer type, a picture of the product doing their job. Got Next and Leadly are public Hanabi examples of product interfaces with a focus. Trade Moai is a public example of an interface organized so a person can scan. The homepage lesson is the same. Show the job the payer recognizes. Save the other jobs for their paths.

## A path for the second and third

A path is a link with a label that the person would use, leading to a page that speaks to them in the first paragraph. It is not a paragraph in the hero that tries to close their sale too.

The second audience often needs a different proof. The clinician needs to see the note, the speed, the day. The office manager needed the price and the migration. Send the clinician to a product screen or a feature page, not to a longer version of the payer's pitch. The wholesale buyer needs terms, minimums, and a person to write. Send them to a page that states those facts. A PDF hidden in a footer is a path you are ashamed of. If the terms are real, make the page real.

The third audience may be smaller and still strategic. Investors, press, and job candidates sometimes get forced into the hero because someone in the company is anxious. Give them the footer or a single about link. The homepage is a selling page. A press kit can exist without occupying the first screen.

Check the paths on a phone. Two text links under the primary button are enough. A row of three identical buttons is the hero compromise coming back in component form. One primary action. The other audiences get text links with specific labels.

Write the secondary pages so they can stand alone. People paste links into Slack. A wholesale page that assumes you read the homepage will confuse the buyer who only received that URL. Repeat the offer in one sentence, then do their job.

## What you refuse to balance

Refuse a headline with a slash. "For owners / managers / teams" is a list of fear. Refuse a rotating banner that gives each audience four seconds. People do not arrive on a schedule that matches your rotation, and reduced motion should not be the only way to see the real offer.

Refuse three equal columns of equal height, equal buttons, and equal adjectives. That layout looks fair in a workshop and reads as unsure on a Tuesday. Fairness to audiences is a path for each. It is not identical square footage in the hero.

Refuse to hide the price logic from the payer because a second audience is price-sensitive. If the payer expects to see how money works, show the shape. The page that explains pricing without a public number is a separate problem. The homepage should not pretend the price does not exist because a student segment might flinch.

Refuse a chatbot as the way you sort audiences. "Are you a clinic, a hospital, or a vendor?" is an interrogation in place of a decision you should have made in the layout. If you truly cannot tell who is visiting, the paths can ask. The hero should still speak to the audience you most need.

Hanabi would settle this in the first working session, on paper or in Figma, before the visual design gets expensive. The site itself is usually Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The ranking of audiences is not a code problem. Code only preserves the rank you wrote down.

## Proof, voice, and the about page

The paying audience judges whether you are real. Use proof they recognize. A named type of customer, a photograph of the work, a constraint you handled. Down the Cove, an ecommerce migration and redesign, would speak to a shop owner. Thomas Bewick, an editorial heritage site, would speak to someone who cares about craft and archives. Ballarat Box Sports would speak to a community brand. Wabisabi would speak to a buyer who wants a calmer object. Put the project that matches the payer on the homepage. Put the others on the work index, or on the secondary path that needs them.

Keep one voice. The clinician page can be more concrete. It should not become a different company. Same type, same button language, same way of admitting a limit. A homepage that is careful and a secondary page that hypes will make the second audience distrust the first.

The about page is where the people behind the offer can stand. Link it once. Do not turn the homepage into an origin story so the third audience feels seen. Origin stories earn their place when they change the decision to buy. Most do not, on the first screen.

## How to test the rank

Read the hero aloud to someone who is the second audience. They should be able to find their path without feeling attacked, and they should not think the product is for them alone. If they cannot find the path, the label is wrong. If they think the hero is for them, you have written the wrong rank, or your sentence is too vague.

Read it to the payer. They should see their job, their proof, and the action without scrolling past a welcome mat. If they ask "is this for hospitals or for us?", the slash headline has returned in disguise.

Look at the queries people use to reach you, if you have them. The phrasing in the hero should match the payer's words. The secondary page can match the second audience's words. One page does not have to rank for every phrasing. Google's helpful-content guidance favors a primary purpose. A homepage with a primary audience is aligned with that. A homepage written to harvest three unrelated queries is a search page wearing a brand.

Review the rank when the business changes, not every time a campaign launches. A seasonal push can have its own page, louder inside the same brand. It should not dethrone the payer for a month unless that month is genuinely when the company makes its year, and even then the other paths should survive.

If the rank is clear and you are about to hire a studio to build it, the next questions are practical. Who does the work, what you will own, how decisions get made, and what done looks like. The piece on [what a founder should ask in the first studio call](/blog/what-a-founder-should-ask-in-the-first-studio-call) is the right next read before you book time.

When you want help choosing the audience that pays and giving the others a real path, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the three sentences. The call should end with a rank, not with a bigger hero.
